clinicalPearls: Postsynaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by biallelic RAPSN variants that impair clustering and anchoring of acetylcholine receptors at the endplate.
Two broad phenotypes occur: an early-onset neonatal form with hypotonia, feeding and respiratory difficulty and arthrogryposis, and a milder late-onset form resembling seronegative myasthenia.
Multiple congenital contractures (arthrogryposis) reflect reduced fetal movement from impaired transmission and are an important clue in the neonatal presentation.
Episodic apnoeic and bulbar crises can be precipitated by febrile illness, so families need an emergency plan even when the child is stable.
Cholinesterase inhibitors are usually effective and are first-line, often with the addition of a potassium-channel modulator such as amifampridine or a beta-agonist in some patients.
A common founder missense variant (in the amino-terminal domain) is frequently seen in patients of European ancestry.
Rapsyn is a postsynaptic scaffolding protein that links acetylcholine receptors to the underlying cytoskeleton, so the receptor itself is normal but poorly concentrated at the endplate.
reference.pathophysiology: Rapsyn (receptor-associated protein of the synapse) is a postsynaptic scaffolding protein that co-localises with acetylcholine receptors and physically tethers them to the subsynaptic cytoskeleton, concentrating receptors within the crests of the junctional folds where they are optimally positioned to respond to released transmitter. Acting downstream of the agrin-LRP4-MuSK-DOK7 pathway, rapsyn is essential for translating that signal into a dense, stable receptor cluster. Biallelic pathogenic RAPSN variants reduce the amount or function of rapsyn so that receptors, although kinetically and structurally normal, fail to aggregate adequately and are present at low density on simplified endplates. The reduced receptor number lowers the safety margin of neuromuscular transmission, producing fatigable weakness that fluctuates and worsens with sustained activity or intercurrent illness. In the fetus, deficient transmission limits movement in utero and can cause arthrogryposis, while postnatally the low endplate receptor density underlies the neonatal hypotonia, bulbar and respiratory difficulty, and the tendency to febrile apnoeic crises; because transmitter release and receptor gating are intact, cholinesterase inhibition that prolongs acetylcholine availability is generally beneficial.
additionalDifferentials: Other postsynaptic congenital myasthenic syndromes, especially acetylcholine receptor subunit deficiencies
Arthrogryposis multiplex congenita from other neuromuscular or connective-tissue causes
Spinal muscular atrophy and congenital myopathies presenting with neonatal hypotonia
Transient neonatal and seronegative autoimmune myasthenia gravis
DOK7 and rapsyn-independent endplate development disorders
Fetal akinesia sequence from central nervous system pathology
additionalInvestigations: Repetitive nerve stimulation demonstrating a decremental response
Single-fibre electromyography showing increased jitter and blocking
Targeted RAPSN sequencing including the common founder variant, or a congenital myasthenic syndrome gene panel
Negative acetylcholine receptor and muscle-specific kinase antibodies to exclude autoimmune disease
Documented clinical and electrophysiological response to a cholinesterase inhibitor
Assessment and imaging of joint contractures where arthrogryposis is present
redFlags: Neonatal respiratory failure or recurrent apnoea, especially with intercurrent fever
Rapidly progressive bulbar weakness with aspiration and secretion pooling
Deterioration during infection requiring ventilatory support
Feeding failure with faltering growth in an infant with hypotonia and contractures
reference.prognosis: Many patients respond well to cholinesterase inhibition and stabilise or improve over childhood, with the milder late-onset phenotype often carrying a good functional outlook. The main hazard remains sudden apnoeic crises during febrile illness, so a rehearsed emergency plan is essential.
pitfalls: Overlooking a treatable neuromuscular junction disorder in an infant labelled only with arthrogryposis
Assuming stability between crises means the child is not at risk during febrile illness
Failing to test for the common founder variant when panel results are initially inconclusive
Not providing a home apnoea and emergency plan for a child prone to febrile crises
references: Standard neuromuscular and paediatric neurology textbooks
Peer-reviewed reviews of congenital myasthenic syndromes
